rows.why: The rows that set this scenario apart are `2d` = 172800000 and `1d0h0m0s0ms` = 86400000. Both depend on whether a day unit exists. The pick adds `d` as 86400000 ms. The plain h/m/s/ms rows are not an open question, and the zero rows also fit item 10, whose pick agrees too.
Item 8 asks whether whitespace around a duration is allowed. The pick trims leading and trailing whitespace, so `  45m\n` parses as 45m = 2700000.

This is a mix of many separate questions: empty (7), bare number (1), fraction (4), sign (5), inner whitespace (8), case (9). No one item's answer settles what the scenario expects. Some rows, such as the leading zero `05s`, the full-width digit `３s` and the unit with no count `ms`, are not asked about by any item.

No item asks whether a count can be larger than the next unit up (`90m` instead of `1h30m`). Item 3 is about unit order and repeated units, not count size. Item 11 is about the form formatting writes, not what parsing accepts.
Item 3 asks whether units must go from largest to smallest and whether a unit may repeat. The pick rejects both with an error, which is what the scenario expects.
Item 6 asks about the upper limit on the parsed total. The pick errors only when the total is above 9007199254740991, so exactly 9007199254740991 parses without error.
Same question as S6. The pick errors when the total is above the limit and checks before adding, so even the huge `99999999999999999999ms` cannot overflow and is rejected.

Item 11 asks how formatting writes values. The pick breaks a value into every non-zero unit from `d` down to `ms`, which gives `1m30s`, `1h30m`, `1d` and `1d1h1m1s1ms`. The `0ms` row also matches item 10's pick.
The same breakdown rule gives `104249991d8h59m991ms`. Item 12's limit rejects only values above 9007199254740991, so this exact value formats without error.
No item asks whether formatting and then parsing gives the same number back. That follows from other choices taken together, not from any one item.

Item 12 asks what formatting does with negative or too-large values. The pick returns an empty string and an error for anything below 0 or above 9007199254740991. That covers -1, 9007199254740992, MinInt64 and MaxInt64. The pick does not say what the error message reads.
